question: How does the Michigan Boater Safety Course define a personal watercraft (PWC)?
choice_a: A small vessel that uses an inboard jet drive as its primary source of propulsion and is designed to be operated by a person sitting, standing, or kneeling on the vessel rather than inside it
choice_b: Any vessel under 26 feet with an outboard motor
choice_c: A vessel that must be operated only while seated inside a cockpit
choice_d: Any vessel propelled by oars or paddles
explanation: A PWC is a small vessel that uses an inboard jet drive as its primary source of propulsion and is designed to be operated by a person or persons sitting, standing, or kneeling on the vessel rather than inside the vessel; the USCG classifies PWCs within the group of inboard vessels less than 16 feet in length.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'What Is a PWC?'

question: How does a jet drive propel a personal watercraft?
choice_a: A submerged propeller pushes the vessel forward and a rudder steers it
choice_b: An engine powers a water pump that sucks up water and forces a jet of water out the back to thrust the vessel forward, with steering done by directing that jet
choice_c: Compressed air is released from tanks to push the vessel forward
choice_d: An outboard motor with a propeller mounted below the waterline
explanation: Jet drives use an engine to power a water pump that sucks up water and forces a jet of water out the back of the vessel to thrust it forward; directing this jet of water steers the vessel.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Jet Drives'

question: On a PWC's jet drive, what is the purpose of the intake grate?
choice_a: It filters fuel before it reaches the engine
choice_b: It cools the exhaust before it exits the hull
choice_c: It is a screening cover over the water intake that prevents large debris from entering
choice_d: It regulates the reserve fuel supply
explanation: The intake grate is a screening cover over the intake opening in the hull, which prevents large debris from entering and damaging the impeller.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Jet Drives'

question: Besides PWC, what other vessels commonly use jet drive propulsion?
choice_a: Only large offshore cargo ships
choice_b: Only sailboats under 16 feet
choice_c: Canoes and kayaks
choice_d: Jet boats, which may have inboard or outboard jet drives and are commonly used for shallow-water conditions
explanation: Jet drives also may power larger vessels, called jet boats, which are commonly used for vessels designed for shallow-water conditions; jet boats can have inboard or outboard jet drives.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Jet Drives'

question: How does a displacement hull move a boat through the water?
choice_a: It pushes the water aside and is designed to cut through the water with very little propulsion, limiting the boat to slower speeds
choice_b: It rises up and glides on top of the water once enough power is applied
choice_c: It relies entirely on wind pressure against a flat bottom
choice_d: It uses a jet of water forced out the stern
explanation: Boats with displacement hulls move through the water by pushing the water aside; a round-bottomed hull shape acts as a displacement hull, and most large cruisers and most sailboats have displacement hulls, which limits them to slower speeds.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Displacement Hulls'

question: What distinguishes a planing hull from a displacement hull?
choice_a: A planing hull can only be used on personal watercraft
choice_b: A planing hull is designed to rise up and glide, or skim, on top of the water once enough power is supplied, rather than continuously pushing water aside
choice_c: A planing hull always has a round bottom like a displacement hull
choice_d: A planing hull cannot exceed displacement speed under any circumstances
explanation: Planing hulls are designed to rise up and glide on top of the water when enough power is supplied, allowing the boat to skim along at high speed; they are typically flat-bottomed or vee-bottomed and are common on small power-driven vessels, PWC, and some sailboats.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Planing Hulls'

question: According to the Michigan Boater Safety Course, what is the 'give-way vessel' in an encounter between two boats?
choice_a: The vessel that has the right to maintain its course and speed no matter what
choice_b: Whichever vessel is traveling faster at the time
choice_c: The vessel that is required to take early and substantial action to keep well away from other vessels by stopping, slowing down, or changing course
choice_d: The vessel closest to shore
explanation: The give-way vessel is the vessel that is required to take early and substantial action to keep well away from other vessels by stopping, slowing down, or changing course.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Rules for Encountering Other Vessels'

question: According to the Michigan Boater Safety Course, what must the 'stand-on vessel' do in an encounter between two boats?
choice_a: Immediately stop its engine and drift
choice_b: Always turn to port to avoid the other vessel
choice_c: Sound five short blasts before doing anything else
choice_d: Maintain its course and speed unless it becomes apparent that the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action
explanation: The stand-on vessel must maintain its course and speed unless it becomes apparent that the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action; if the stand-on vessel must then take action, it should not turn toward the give-way vessel or cross in front of it.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Rules for Encountering Other Vessels' / 'Power-Driven Vessel Encountering Power-Driven Vessel'

question: When changing course or speed to avoid another vessel, how should the change be made?
choice_a: Large enough to be readily apparent to the other vessel, avoiding a series of small changes
choice_b: As small and gradual as possible so the other operator does not notice
choice_c: Only after sounding the danger signal five times
choice_d: It does not matter, as long as a collision is avoided
explanation: Any change in course or speed made to avoid collision should be large enough to be readily apparent to another vessel; a series of small changes should be avoided.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Rules for Encountering Other Vessels'

question: What is the general exception to the navigation rules when encountering a vessel with less maneuverability than your own?
choice_a: Your vessel is automatically the stand-on vessel regardless of maneuverability
choice_b: The other, less maneuverable vessel will usually be the stand-on vessel
choice_c: Whichever vessel is registered in Michigan has the right of way
choice_d: The navigation rules do not apply to vessels with limited maneuverability
explanation: If you approach a vessel that has less maneuverability than your vessel, the other vessel will usually be the stand-on vessel.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Exceptions to the Navigation Rules'

question: Under what circumstance may an operator depart from the standard navigation rules?
choice_a: Whenever the operator believes it will save time
choice_b: Only if written permission is obtained from the Michigan DNR in advance
choice_c: When dangers of navigation, risk of collision, or special conditions including the limitations of the boats involved make a departure necessary to avoid immediate danger
choice_d: Navigation rules can never be departed from under any circumstance
explanation: Every operator is responsible for avoiding a collision; in complying with the navigation rules, operators must consider all dangers of navigation, risk of collision, and any special conditions, including the limitations of the boats involved, which may make a departure from the navigation rules necessary to avoid immediate danger.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Exceptions to the Navigation Rules'

question: Under the navigation rules, which of the following is NOT considered a vessel 'engaged in fishing' with restricted maneuverability?
choice_a: A vessel fishing with nets that restrict its ability to maneuver
choice_b: A vessel fishing with trawls that restrict its ability to maneuver
choice_c: A vessel fishing with long lines that restrict its ability to maneuver
choice_d: A vessel fishing with trolling lines or other fishing equipment that does not restrict maneuverability
explanation: A vessel engaged in fishing is any vessel fishing with nets, lines, trawls, or other fishing equipment that restricts maneuverability; this does not include a vessel fishing with trolling lines or other fishing equipment that does not restrict maneuverability.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Navigation Rules: Definitions'

question: According to the navigation rules' definitions, when is a vessel considered 'underway'?
choice_a: When it is not anchored, tied to shore, or aground
choice_b: Only when its engine is running
choice_c: Only when it is moving faster than idle speed
choice_d: Whenever a person is aboard the vessel
explanation: 'Underway' is defined as not anchored, tied to shore, or aground.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Navigation Rules: Definitions'

question: According to the navigation rules, when does 'risk of collision' exist?
choice_a: Only when both vessels are within 100 feet of each other
choice_b: When an approaching vessel continues on a collision course with a bearing that does not change, or anytime you are approaching a very large vessel
choice_c: Only after one operator sounds a warning signal
choice_d: Only in restricted visibility conditions
explanation: Risk of collision exists any time an approaching vessel continues on a collision course, meaning the bearing of the approaching vessel does not change, or anytime you are approaching a very large vessel.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Navigation Rules: Definitions'

question: How is a 'power-driven vessel' defined under the navigation rules?
choice_a: Only a vessel with an outboard motor mounted on the transom
choice_b: Any vessel that is not a personal watercraft
choice_c: Any vessel propelled by machinery, including a sailboat using an engine
choice_d: Any vessel over 26 feet in length
explanation: A power-driven vessel is defined as any vessel propelled by machinery, including a sailboat using an engine.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Navigation Rules: Definitions'

question: For purposes of the navigation rules, when is a boat considered a 'sailing vessel' rather than a 'power-driven vessel'?
choice_a: Any time it has a mast and sail installed, even while motoring
choice_b: Only if it has no engine installed at all
choice_c: Whenever it is registered as a sailboat with the state
choice_d: When it is under sail and has no engine in use
explanation: A sailing vessel is defined as any vessel under sail and with no engine in use; a sailboat running its engine is legally a power-driven vessel.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Navigation Rules: Definitions'

question: Under the federal Inland Navigation Rules that apply on Michigan's Great Lakes waters, at what point is a vessel considered to be 'overtaking' another?
choice_a: When coming up with another vessel from a direction more than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam, such that at night only the other vessel's sternlight would be visible
choice_b: Whenever it approaches from directly ahead
choice_c: Only when it is traveling more than twice the speed of the other vessel
choice_d: Whenever it is within 50 feet of another vessel
explanation: Under Rule 13 of the Inland Navigation Rules, a vessel is overtaking when coming up with another vessel from a direction more than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam -- a position from which, at night, she would be able to see only the sternlight of the vessel she is overtaking, not either of her sidelights.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.13, Inland Navigation Rules (Rule 13, Overtaking); Great Lakes are Inland Rules waters under 33 CFR Part 80

question: Once a vessel is classified as the overtaking vessel, what happens if the bearing between the two vessels later changes?
choice_a: It automatically becomes a crossing situation and the stand-on/give-way roles reverse
choice_b: The overtaking vessel remains the give-way vessel until it is finally past and clear, even if the bearing changes so the situation would otherwise look like a crossing situation
choice_c: Both vessels become stand-on vessels
choice_d: The rules no longer apply once the vessels are within 22.5 degrees of each other
explanation: Any subsequent alteration of the bearing between the two vessels does not make the overtaking vessel a crossing vessel, nor does it relieve the overtaking vessel of its duty to keep clear until it is finally past and clear of the vessel being overtaken.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.13, Inland Navigation Rules (Rule 13, Overtaking)

question: When a power-driven vessel encounters a sailing vessel under sail (meeting head-on or crossing), which vessel is the give-way vessel?
choice_a: The sailing vessel, which must give way to the power-driven vessel
choice_b: Neither; both must hold course and speed
choice_c: The power-driven vessel, which must give way to the sailing vessel
choice_d: Whichever vessel is larger
explanation: If operating a power-driven vessel, you must always give way to a sailing vessel; the power-driven vessel is the give-way vessel and the sailing vessel is the stand-on vessel, unless the sailing vessel is overtaking.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Power-Driven Vessel Encountering Sailing Vessel'

question: A sailboat under sail is overtaking a power-driven vessel. Which vessel must give way?
choice_a: The power-driven vessel, because sailing vessels always have right-of-way over power-driven vessels
choice_b: Neither vessel needs to give way during an overtaking situation
choice_c: The power-driven vessel, because it is being approached from behind
choice_d: The sailboat, because the vessel that is overtaking another is always the give-way vessel regardless of whether it is a sailing vessel or a power-driven vessel
explanation: The vessel that is overtaking another vessel is the give-way vessel, regardless of whether it is a sailing vessel or a power-driven vessel; this overtaking rule overrides the usual power-vs-sail priority.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Power-Driven Vessel Encountering Sailing Vessel'

question: In addition to sailing vessels, a power-driven vessel must give way to which of the following, ranked ahead of sailing vessels in the responsibility hierarchy?
choice_a: Any vessel not under command, any vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver, and any vessel engaged in commercial fishing
choice_b: Any vessel that departed the dock earlier that day
choice_c: Any vessel with a larger engine
choice_d: Any vessel flying a solid-color flag
explanation: A power-driven vessel must give way, in order of priority, to any vessel not under command, any vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver, a vessel engaged in commercial fishing, and then a sailing vessel (unless the sailing vessel is overtaking).
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Responsibilities Between Vessels'

question: What is an example of a vessel that is 'restricted in its ability to maneuver' under the navigation rules?
choice_a: Any vessel operating at idle speed
choice_b: A vessel towing, laying cable, or picking up navigation markers, or a vessel constrained by its draft
choice_c: Any vessel with fewer than three passengers aboard
choice_d: Any vessel operating after sunset
explanation: A vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver includes a vessel towing, laying cable, or picking up navigation markers, or a vessel constrained by its draft.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Responsibilities Between Vessels'

question: Even a sailing vessel under sail is not the stand-on vessel against which other vessels?
choice_a: Any other sailboat, regardless of wind direction
choice_b: Any PWC, regardless of the situation
choice_c: Any vessel not under command, any vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver, and any vessel engaged in commercial fishing
choice_d: Any vessel under 16 feet in length
explanation: Sailing vessels must yield to any vessel not under command, any vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver, and vessels engaged in commercial fishing -- these vessels outrank sailing vessels in the responsibility hierarchy.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Responsibilities Between Vessels'

question: Two sailboats under sail are approaching each other with the wind on the same side of both boats. Which is the stand-on vessel?
choice_a: The windward sailing vessel (the one further upwind)
choice_b: Whichever boat is closer to shore
choice_c: Neither; both must alter course simultaneously
choice_d: The leeward sailing vessel (the one further downwind)
explanation: When two sailing vessels have the wind on the same side, the leeward sailing vessel is the stand-on vessel and the windward vessel must give way.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Sailing Vessel Encountering Sailing Vessel'

question: Two sailboats under sail are approaching each other with the wind on different sides of each boat. Which is the stand-on vessel?
choice_a: The sailing vessel with the wind on its starboard (right) side
choice_b: The sailing vessel with the wind on its port (left) side
choice_c: Whichever vessel has the larger sail area
choice_d: Whichever vessel is moving faster
explanation: When two sailing vessels have the wind on different sides, the sailing vessel with the wind on its starboard (right) side is the stand-on vessel.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Sailing Vessel Encountering Sailing Vessel'

question: A sailboat has the wind on its port side and cannot determine whether an approaching sailboat to windward has the wind on its port or starboard side. What should the operator do?
choice_a: Maintain course and speed because it is automatically the stand-on vessel
choice_b: Yield to the windward vessel as a safety precaution
choice_c: Sound the danger signal and continue on course
choice_d: Assume the other vessel has the wind on its port side
explanation: If a sailboat with the wind on its port side cannot determine which side the wind is on for an approaching windward vessel, it should yield to that windward vessel as a safety precaution.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Sailing Vessel Encountering Sailing Vessel'

question: Two PWC are meeting head-on. What should both operators do?
choice_a: Both should turn to port (the left)
choice_b: One must stop completely while the other passes
choice_c: Neither is the stand-on vessel; both vessels should turn to starboard (the right)
choice_d: Both should maintain course and speed
explanation: When two PWC meet head-on, neither vessel is the stand-on vessel; both vessels should turn to starboard (the right).
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'PWC Encountering PWC'

question: Two PWC are on crossing paths. Which PWC is the give-way vessel?
choice_a: The PWC on the operator's starboard (right) side
choice_b: Whichever PWC is closer to the nearest shore
choice_c: Whichever PWC was launched first that day
choice_d: The PWC on the operator's port (left) side
explanation: When two PWC are on crossing paths, the PWC on the operator's port (left) side is the give-way vessel, and the PWC on the operator's starboard (right) side is the stand-on vessel.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'PWC Encountering PWC'

question: One PWC is overtaking another PWC. Which PWC is responsible for avoiding a collision?
choice_a: The overtaking PWC, which is the give-way vessel; the PWC being overtaken is the stand-on vessel
choice_b: The PWC being overtaken, since it should speed up to get clear
choice_c: Both PWC share equal responsibility with no give-way vessel
choice_d: Whichever PWC operator is older
explanation: The PWC that is overtaking another PWC is the give-way vessel, and the PWC being overtaken is the stand-on vessel.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'PWC Encountering PWC'

question: What speed must every vessel maintain while operating in restricted visibility, such as fog?
choice_a: The vessel's normal cruising speed
choice_b: A safe speed appropriate to the conditions of restricted visibility
choice_c: The maximum speed the vessel is capable of, to clear the area quickly
choice_d: There is no speed requirement in restricted visibility
explanation: Every vessel must proceed at a safe speed given the conditions of restricted visibility.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Operating During Restricted Visibility'

question: In restricted visibility, what must a power-driven vessel's engines be ready to do?
choice_a: Run at full throttle continuously
choice_b: Shut down automatically after two minutes
choice_c: Maneuver immediately
choice_d: Switch to reserve fuel
explanation: A power-driven vessel operating in restricted visibility must have its engines ready to maneuver immediately.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Operating During Restricted Visibility'

question: If, in restricted visibility, you hear another vessel's fog signal apparently ahead of you and risk of collision exists, what should you do?
choice_a: Increase speed to pass the area more quickly
choice_b: Turn off your own engine entirely and drift
choice_c: Maintain your exact current speed and heading
choice_d: Reduce speed to the minimum at which the vessel can be kept on course, reducing to idle speed if necessary
explanation: When you hear another vessel's fog signal apparently forward of your beam, are in a close-quarters situation, or detect another vessel by radar and risk of collision exists, you should reduce speed to the minimum at which the vessel can be kept on course, and if necessary, reduce to idle speed.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Operating During Restricted Visibility'

question: Which of the following conditions is included in the course's definition of 'restricted visibility'?
choice_a: Fog, mist, falling snow, heavy rainstorms, or sandstorms
choice_b: Only complete darkness with no moon
choice_c: Only visibility under 5,280 feet during daylight
choice_d: Only conditions officially declared by the National Weather Service
explanation: Restricted visibility includes fog, mist, falling snow, heavy rainstorms, sandstorms, or similar conditions that affect the ability to see other vessels.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Operating During Restricted Visibility'

question: What color are sidelights, and what is their purpose?
choice_a: Both white; they mark the bow of the vessel
choice_b: Red and green; they are visible to another vessel approaching from the side or head-on
choice_c: Blue and amber; they identify the vessel as a law enforcement boat
choice_d: Solid yellow; they indicate the vessel is towing
explanation: Sidelights are red and green lights that are visible to another vessel approaching from the side or head-on; red marks the port (left) side and green marks the starboard (right) side.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Common Navigation Lights'

question: From what viewing angle is a vessel's sternlight visible?
choice_a: From any direction, all the way around the vessel
choice_b: Only from directly ahead of the vessel
choice_c: Only from behind or nearly behind the vessel
choice_d: Only from the port side
explanation: The sternlight is a white light that can be seen only from behind, or nearly behind, the vessel.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Common Navigation Lights'

question: On vessels less than 39.4 feet in length, how may the masthead light and sternlight be combined?
choice_a: They may never be combined regardless of vessel length
choice_b: Into a single red light visible from astern only
choice_c: Into a flashing amber beacon
choice_d: Into a single all-round white light that can be seen by other vessels from any direction
explanation: On power-driven vessels less than 39.4 feet in length, the masthead light and sternlight may be combined into a single all-round white light that can be seen by other vessels from any direction; larger vessels require the lights to be separate.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Common Navigation Lights'

question: What light configuration does a commercial vessel typically display while towing or pushing a barge?
choice_a: One or more yellow lights in place of a sternlight, and there may be an unlit gap of several hundred yards between the lights on the bow and stern of the composite unit
choice_b: A single flashing blue light on the bow
choice_c: No lights at all if the tow is under 50 feet
choice_d: Two red lights stacked vertically on the stern only
explanation: When commercial vessels are towing or pushing a barge, they display one or more yellow lights in place of a sternlight; there may be an unlit space of several hundred yards between the lights displayed on the bow and stern of the composite formed by the commercial vessel and its barge(s).
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Towing Lights on Commercial Vessels'

question: For a power-driven vessel less than 26 feet long underway at night, what visibility distance is required for its sidelights?
choice_a: Visible from a distance of at least five miles away
choice_b: Visible from a distance of at least one mile away
choice_c: Visible from a distance of at least 500 feet away
choice_d: No specific distance is required as long as they are on
explanation: A power-driven vessel less than 26 feet long must display red and green sidelights visible from a distance of at least one mile away, along with either an all-round white light or a masthead light and sternlight visible from at least two miles away.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Required Lights: Power-Driven Vessels When Underway'

question: For a power-driven vessel 26 feet or longer, where must the masthead light be positioned relative to the sidelights?
choice_a: Lower than the sidelights
choice_b: At exactly the same height as the sidelights
choice_c: Higher than the sidelights
choice_d: Position relative to sidelights is not specified for any vessel
explanation: On a power-driven vessel 26 feet or longer, the masthead light and sternlight must be visible from at least two miles away, with the masthead light positioned higher than the sidelights.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Required Lights: Power-Driven Vessels When Underway'

question: An unpowered (sailing) vessel 26 feet or longer must display sidelights and a sternlight visible from what distances?
choice_a: Sidelights visible at least one mile away and a sternlight visible at least two miles away, the same as a power-driven vessel
choice_b: Sidelights and sternlight both visible at least five miles away
choice_c: No lights are required on any sailing vessel
choice_d: Sidelights visible at least two miles away and a sternlight visible at least three miles away
explanation: An unpowered vessel 26 feet or longer, such as a sailboat under sail, must display red and green sidelights visible from at least two miles away and a sternlight visible from at least three miles away -- greater distances than required for power-driven vessels of the same length.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Required Lights: Unpowered Vessels 26 Feet or Longer When Underway'

question: What lighting option is available to an unpowered vessel less than 26 feet long (such as a small sailboat or rowboat) if it is not practical to install permanent navigation lights?
choice_a: Have on hand at least one lantern or flashlight shining a white light
choice_b: The vessel may not be operated at night under any circumstances
choice_c: A single red flashing light is an acceptable substitute
choice_d: No light of any kind is required if the vessel is under 16 feet
explanation: An unpowered vessel less than 26 feet long should, if practical, exhibit the lights required for unpowered vessels 26 feet or longer; if that is not practical, it must have on hand at least one lantern or flashlight shining a white light.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Required Lights: Unpowered Vessels Less Than 26 Feet When Underway'

question: Besides between sunset and sunrise, when else must a vessel's navigation lights be displayed?
choice_a: Only on federal holidays
choice_b: During periods of restricted visibility such as fog or heavy rain
choice_c: Only when the vessel is docked
choice_d: Navigation lights are never required during daylight hours under any condition
explanation: Navigation lights must be displayed when away from the dock between sunset and sunrise, and also during periods of restricted visibility such as fog or heavy rain.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Overview of Navigation Lights Law'

question: Who is legally permitted to use blue or red flashing lights on a vessel?
choice_a: Any vessel operator who wants extra visibility at night
choice_b: Any vessel towing a skier
choice_c: Law enforcement vessels only
choice_d: Any vessel over 26 feet in length
explanation: Blue or red flashing lights are restricted to use by law enforcement vessels only; no other lights that may be mistaken for required navigation lights may be exhibited.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Overview of Navigation Lights Law'

question: How long does a 'short blast' of a vessel's horn or whistle last, according to the Michigan Boater Safety Course?
choice_a: About ten seconds
choice_b: About 30 seconds
choice_c: There is no defined duration for a short blast
choice_d: About one second
explanation: A short blast lasts about one second, while a prolonged blast lasts 4 to 6 seconds.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Common Sound Signals'

question: What does one short blast of a vessel's horn mean when signaling another vessel during an encounter?
choice_a: I intend to pass you on my port (left) side
choice_b: I intend to pass you on my starboard (right) side
choice_c: I am operating in reverse
choice_d: I am in distress
explanation: One short blast means, 'I intend to pass you on my port (left) side.'
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Sound Signals Used for Encountering Situations'

question: What does two short blasts of a vessel's horn mean when signaling another vessel during an encounter?
choice_a: I intend to pass you on my port (left) side
choice_b: I intend to pass you on my starboard (right) side
choice_c: I am backing up
choice_d: I do not understand or agree with your proposed maneuver
explanation: Two short blasts mean, 'I intend to pass you on my starboard (right) side.'
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Sound Signals Used for Encountering Situations'

question: If another vessel sounds one or two short blasts to signal a passing intention, what should the receiving vessel do if it agrees with the proposed maneuver?
choice_a: Immediately stop its engine
choice_b: Sound five short blasts to confirm
choice_c: Sound the same signal in response
choice_d: Flash its navigation lights three times
explanation: When one vessel signals its passing intention, the other vessel should sound the same signal if it agrees with the proposed maneuver.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Examples of Sound Signals Used for Encountering Situations'

question: What does three short blasts of a vessel's horn mean?
choice_a: I intend to overtake you on your port side
choice_b: I am approaching a blind bend
choice_c: Danger -- I do not understand your intentions
choice_d: I am operating astern propulsion (backing up)
explanation: Three short blasts mean, 'I am operating astern propulsion,' commonly understood to mean the vessel is backing up.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Sound Signals Used for Encountering Situations'

question: When should an operator sound one prolonged blast as a warning signal?
choice_a: For example, when coming around a blind bend or when leaving a dock or slip
choice_b: Only when the vessel is sinking
choice_c: Only after docking has been completed
choice_d: Whenever passing a marina at any speed
explanation: One prolonged blast is a warning signal, used for example when coming around a blind bend or when leaving the dock.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Sound Signals Used to Alert or Warn'

question: What does five or more short, rapid blasts of a horn signal to another vessel?
choice_a: A friendly greeting between vessels
choice_b: Danger, or disagreement with the other vessel's intended maneuver
choice_c: A request for the other vessel to stop for an inspection
choice_d: That the sounding vessel intends to overtake on the starboard side
explanation: Five or more short, rapid blasts is the danger signal, used to indicate danger or disagreement with another vessel's proposed maneuver.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Sound Signals Used to Alert or Warn'

question: In restricted visibility, what sound signal must an underway power-driven vessel sound, and how often?
choice_a: Three short blasts at intervals of not more than one minute
choice_b: Continuous sounding of the horn without pause
choice_c: One prolonged blast at intervals of not more than two minutes
choice_d: No sound signal is required if radar is on board
explanation: A power-driven vessel underway in restricted visibility must sound one prolonged blast at intervals of not more than two minutes.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Sound Signals Used to Alert or Warn'

question: In restricted visibility, what sound signal must an underway sailing vessel sound, and how often?
choice_a: One prolonged blast only, at intervals of not more than two minutes, identical to a power-driven vessel
choice_b: Five short blasts every minute
choice_c: Two prolonged blasts every 30 seconds
choice_d: One prolonged blast plus two short blasts, at intervals of not more than two minutes
explanation: A sailing vessel underway in restricted visibility must sound one prolonged blast plus two short blasts at intervals of not more than two minutes, distinguishing it from a power-driven vessel's signal.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Sound Signals Used to Alert or Warn'

question: On Michigan's state waters, what sound-producing device is required for a vessel 16 to less than 26 feet long operating under engine power?
choice_a: A whistle capable of producing a blast of two seconds or more, audible for at least one-half mile
choice_b: A ship's bell only, with no whistle required
choice_c: No sound-producing device is required for vessels under 26 feet
choice_d: A siren audible for at least ten miles
explanation: On state waters, a vessel 16 to less than 26 feet long operating under engine power must carry a whistle capable of producing a blast of two seconds or more that is audible for at least one-half mile.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Requirements to Have Sound-Producing Devices'

question: On Michigan's state waters, what audible range is required for the whistle on a vessel 26 feet or longer operating under engine power?
choice_a: Audible for at least one-half mile, the same as smaller vessels
choice_b: Audible for at least one mile
choice_c: Audible for at least 100 yards
choice_d: No specific audible range is required
explanation: On state waters, a vessel 26 feet or longer operating under engine power must have a whistle audible for at least one mile.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Requirements to Have Sound-Producing Devices'

question: On federally controlled waters, what sound-producing device is required for a vessel less than 39.4 feet (12 meters), including a PWC?
choice_a: The human voice alone is sufficient
choice_b: No sound-producing device is required for any vessel under 39.4 feet
choice_c: An efficient sound device such as a handheld air horn, an athletic whistle, or an installed horn; the human voice is not acceptable
choice_d: A ship's bell only
explanation: On federally controlled waters, a vessel less than 39.4 feet (12 meters), including a PWC, must carry an efficient sound device such as a handheld air horn, an athletic whistle, or an installed horn; the human voice is not acceptable.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Requirements to Have Sound-Producing Devices'

question: On lateral markers of the U.S. Aids to Navigation System, in which direction do the numbers generally increase?
choice_a: As a boater heads out toward the open sea
choice_b: Numbers reset to zero every mile regardless of direction
choice_c: Numbers decrease as a boater heads upstream
choice_d: As a boater returns from the open sea or heads upstream
explanation: Numbers on lateral markers usually increase consecutively as a boater returns from the open sea or heads upstream.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Lateral Markers: Colors and Numbers'

question: What do green colors, green lights, and odd numbers on lateral markers indicate?
choice_a: The edge of the channel on your port (left) side as you enter from the open sea or head upstream
choice_b: The edge of the channel on your starboard (right) side as you enter from the open sea or head upstream
choice_c: An area closed to all vessels
choice_d: A mid-channel or fairway with unobstructed water on all sides
explanation: Green colors, green lights, and odd numbers mark the edge of the channel on your port (left) side as you enter from the open sea or head upstream.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Lateral Markers: Colors and Numbers'

question: What shape and color are 'cans' as lateral markers?
choice_a: Red cone-shaped buoys marked with even numbers
choice_b: Green cylindrical-shaped buoys marked with odd numbers
choice_c: White buoys with orange bands
choice_d: Yellow spherical buoys
explanation: Can buoys are cylindrical-shaped buoys with green markings and odd numbers, marking the port side of the channel as a boater enters from the open sea or heads upstream.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Lateral Markers: Shapes'

question: On a junction (preferred channel) marker showing both red and green bands, what does it mean if green is on top?
choice_a: The preferred channel is to the left
choice_b: The channel is closed in both directions
choice_c: The preferred channel is to the right
choice_d: The marker indicates a mooring area, not a channel junction
explanation: On a junction marker combining red and green, if green is on top, the preferred channel is to the right; if red is on top, the preferred channel is to the left.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Lateral Markers: Colors and Numbers'

question: What are lateral daymarks (permanent signs attached to posts in the water) that serve the same function as buoys?
choice_a: Only round white signs are used as daymarks
choice_b: Daymarks are always unlit and never used at night
choice_c: Daymarks only appear on the Western Rivers System
choice_d: Red triangles function as the equivalent of nun buoys, and green squares function as the equivalent of can buoys
explanation: Daymarks are permanently placed signs attached to structures such as posts in the water; red triangles are the daymark equivalent of nun buoys and green squares are the daymark equivalent of can buoys, and daymarks may also be lit.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Lateral Markers: Other Kinds of Buoys and Markers'

question: How can a lighted buoy on the U.S. Aids to Navigation System be identified at night?
choice_a: It uses the same lateral marker shape, color, and number as an unlit buoy, plus a matching colored light
choice_b: All lighted buoys display only white lights regardless of channel side
choice_c: Lighted buoys always flash in Morse code to spell out the channel name
choice_d: Lighted buoys are only used on Great Lakes connecting channels, never elsewhere
explanation: Lighted buoys use the same lateral marker shapes, colors, and numbers as standard buoys, with a matching colored light added so the marker can be identified at night.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Lateral Markers: Other Kinds of Buoys and Markers'

question: What does a non-lateral marker shaped like a plain square indicate?
choice_a: Danger from rocks or shoals requiring extreme caution
choice_b: Information such as places to find food, supplies, and repairs, and directions or distances
choice_c: A controlled area such as a no-wake or ski zone
choice_d: An area completely off-limits to all vessels
explanation: Square non-lateral markers provide information such as places to find food, supplies, and repairs, and they give directions, distances, and other non-regulatory information.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Common Non-Lateral Markers'

question: What does a non-lateral marker shaped like a plain diamond (not crossed) indicate?
choice_a: A place to find food, supplies, or repairs
choice_b: A controlled area such as a speed limit zone
choice_c: A danger such as rocks, shoals, construction, dams, or stumps, requiring boaters to proceed with caution and keep a safe distance
choice_d: An exclusion area off-limits to all vessels
explanation: Diamond-shaped non-lateral markers warn of dangers such as rocks, shoals, construction, dams, or stumps; boaters should always proceed with caution and keep a safe distance.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Common Non-Lateral Markers'

question: What does a non-lateral marker shaped like a circle indicate?
choice_a: An area off-limits to all vessels, such as a swimming area
choice_b: Directions and distances to nearby marinas
choice_c: Danger from an obstruction just below the surface
choice_d: A controlled area such as a no-wake zone, idle-speed zone, speed limit, or ski zone
explanation: Circle-shaped non-lateral markers indicate a controlled area, such as no wake, idle speed, a speed limit, or a ski zone.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Common Non-Lateral Markers'

question: What color scheme and meaning does a safe water marker have on the U.S. Aids to Navigation System?
choice_a: White with red vertical stripes, indicating unobstructed water on all sides; it may be passed on either side and marks a mid-channel or fairway
choice_b: White with blue vertical stripes, indicating a swimming area
choice_c: Solid red, indicating a hazard that must be passed only on the right
choice_d: White with black vertical stripes, indicating an obstruction to navigation
explanation: A safe water marker is white with red vertical stripes and indicates unobstructed water on all sides; these mark mid-channels or fairways and may be passed on either side.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Other Non-Lateral Markers'

question: Of all the buoys in the U.S. Aids to Navigation System, which are the only ones a boater may legally tie up to?
choice_a: Any lateral marker, including cans and nuns
choice_b: Mooring buoys (white with a blue horizontal band)
choice_c: Inland Waters Obstruction Markers
choice_d: Safe water markers
explanation: Mooring buoys, which are white with a blue horizontal band, are the only buoys a boater may legally tie up to; they are typically found in marinas and other areas where vessels are permitted to anchor or moor.
source_note: Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan), 'Other Non-Lateral Markers'
